strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: controllable adverse-weather editing for autonomous-driving imagery, with a physically motivated intrinsic-space formulation rather than direct pixel-space translation.

The proposed decomposition into material/geometry maps plus weather-dependent irradiance is a sensible design choice, and the intrinsic map-aware attention mechanism is a plausible contribution for improving spatial correspondence in large outdoor scenes.

The experimental section compares against several relevant pixel editing, weather restoration, and diffusion rendering baselines. Reported results include prompt/structure metrics, synthetic inverse-rendering metrics, qualitative comparisons, user study results, and downstream detection/segmentation gains on ACDC.
The WeatherSynthetic dataset, if released with intrinsic maps as claimed, would likely be useful for future work on outdoor inverse rendering and weather-aware generation.
Ablations for IMAA and WeatherReal support that both components contribute to the reported performance.
weaknesses: The strongest quantitative inverse-rendering evidence is on the authors' synthetic dataset. Real-world intrinsic-map quality is mostly qualitative or supplementary, so the central claim of robust real-world decomposition under adverse weather is not fully established.

WeatherReal is constructed using the proposed inverse renderer for pseudo-labels and Flux-Kontext for weather editing, which creates possible circularity and makes it hard to separate dataset quality, model bias, and true supervision. More independent validation of pseudo-label accuracy is needed.

The method's novelty is somewhat incremental: it combines a pretrained diffusion model, CLIP-space prompt interpolation, feature distillation, and attention biasing. The paper would benefit from clearer evidence that IMAA is the decisive technical advance rather than dataset/domain adaptation and model scale.

Editing evaluation relies heavily on CLIP-S, PickScore, and DINO-S, which are imperfect proxies for physical correctness and object/material preservation. Human preference is reported but only briefly, with details deferred to the supplement.

The downstream ACDC results are promising but under-analyzed. The paper does not sufficiently compare against all restoration/editing baselines in the downstream table or rule out that improvements come from distribution/style changes rather than physically faithful weather correction.

Reproducibility is limited in the main paper: important training details, feature distillation details, heuristic training for IMAA, user-study setup, and dataset filtering/manual checking protocol are either underspecified or deferred to supplementary material. The dataset is promised for release but not yet available in the manuscript.
The paper acknowledges lack of temporal consistency, which is a significant limitation for autonomous driving use cases where video is the natural input modality.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and practically relevant problem: controllable weather editing for autonomous-driving imagery, where preserving geometry and scene content matters more than generic image-editing aesthetics.

The intrinsic-space framing is a reasonable direction. Separating weather-invariant geometry/material maps from weather-varying illumination could, in principle, provide better control than direct pixel-space editing.

The manuscript includes a broad set of comparisons: pixel-space editors, weather restoration methods, inverse/forward rendering methods, ablations for IMAA and WeatherReal, a small user study, and downstream detection/segmentation experiments on ACDC.

The reported quantitative gains on WeatherSynthetic inverse rendering are large, and the ablation suggests that the intrinsic map-aware attention improves decomposition metrics over the same model without IMAA.
The figures communicate the intended behavior clearly, and the limitation on temporal inconsistency is acknowledged.
weaknesses: The central empirical support is not fully convincing. The strongest decomposition results are on the authors' own synthetic dataset, using the same rendering setup and intrinsic-map definitions that train the model. This makes the very large PSNR/SSIM gains difficult to interpret as evidence of general intrinsic decomposition ability rather than dataset-specific fitting.

The real-world supervision pipeline is circular and weakly justified: WeatherReal intrinsic maps are generated by the authors' inverse renderer, filtered manually, and augmented with Flux-Kontext edits. This is useful engineering, but it undermines claims that the model learns physically meaningful real-world intrinsic maps from reliable annotations.

Evaluation on real images is mostly qualitative or based on proxy metrics. CLIP-S, PickScore, and DINO-S are not sufficient to establish physically consistent weather editing, material preservation, or illumination correctness. The paper repeatedly makes physical/geometry-preservation claims without direct real-world ground truth or stronger consistency tests.

The comparison protocol appears uneven. Some baselines are generic image editors, some are restoration models, and some are rendering methods with different inputs and assumptions. For example, DiffusionRenderer is given environment lighting while the proposed method is prompt-conditioned; weather restoration baselines are penalized for not changing surface snow or illumination, which is partly outside their task definition.

The downstream ACDC experiment is underdeveloped. Editing validation images to sunny conditions and then evaluating DETR/SegFormer can show a preprocessing effect, but it does not by itself demonstrate robust autonomous-driving perception. The paper does not sufficiently analyze whether the editor changes label-relevant content, hallucinates/removes objects, or leaks biases that make evaluation optimistic.

The technical method is underspecified in the main paper. Important details such as the exact SD3.5 adaptation, training objectives, map parameterization, loss weights, feature distillation, IMAA training schedule, filtering criteria, and dataset splits are either vague or deferred to supplementary material. This substantially hurts reproducibility.

The claimed novelty is moderate. The work combines diffusion-based inverse/forward rendering, intrinsic editing, CLIP prompt interpolation, DINO features, and attention biasing. The resulting system may be useful, but the core algorithmic ideas appear incremental relative to prior diffusion intrinsic/rendering and image-editing approaches.

The dataset contribution is potentially valuable but insufficiently documented. Licensing, release conditions, manual quality-control procedures, pseudo-label reliability, and train/test separation are not described enough to assess reproducibility or possible contamination with evaluation data.

The ablation evidence is narrow. IMAA is compared only to a removal of IMAA, and WeatherReal is shown mainly qualitatively. There is little analysis of which components drive gains, whether CLIP-space interpolation is better than simpler prompt/intensity controls, or how sensitive the method is to intrinsic-map errors.

The paper's claims are stronger than the evidence supports. Phrases about physically grounded estimations, preserving material and geometry, and correcting environmental distortions are not matched by sufficiently rigorous validation, especially on real-world data. Overall, the work has an appealing direction and some promising results, but the current manuscript does not provide enough reliable evidence for acceptance at CVPR.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: controllable weather editing for autonomous-driving scenes, where preserving geometry/materials is more valuable than generic pixel-space translation.

The intrinsic-space formulation is compelling. Decomposing images into albedo, normals, roughness, metallicity, and irradiance gives a clearer mechanism for separating weather/illumination changes from scene structure, and the qualitative examples support this motivation.

The proposed intrinsic map-aware attention is a plausible technical contribution. The ablation in Table 3 shows consistent gains over the no-IMAA variant across decomposition metrics, especially for normals and irradiance.

The experimental scope is fairly broad: comparisons include pixel-space editing methods, weather restoration methods, rendering/inverse-rendering baselines, a user study, fine-grained weather control, and downstream detection/segmentation on ACDC.

The reported results are strong. Table 3 shows large quantitative gains on WeatherSynthetic, Table 1 shows competitive or best text/weather alignment while maintaining better structure than most editing baselines, and Table 2 reports meaningful downstream improvements after weather correction.
The new WeatherSynthetic and WeatherReal datasets, if released as promised, would be useful resources for weather-aware rendering and autonomous-driving robustness research.
weaknesses: The strongest quantitative inverse-rendering evidence is on the authors' synthetic benchmark, so it is hard to separate method quality from dataset/rendering-domain fit. Real-world inverse rendering is mainly qualitative or relegated to supplementary consistency checks, with no ground-truth real evaluation.

WeatherReal is constructed using the authors' inverse renderer plus Flux-Kontext edits and manual filtering. This is pragmatic, but it creates a partially self-generated training source whose label quality, biases, filtering criteria, and possible failure modes are not sufficiently characterized in the main paper.

The evaluation of downstream benefits is promising but incomplete. Table 2 compares original ACDC images against images processed by WeatherDiffusion, but does not quantitatively compare against restoration baselines such as AWRaCLe or Histoformer, even though Figure 8 argues qualitatively that those methods are weaker.

Some baselines may not be equally specialized or equally adapted. IID/RGB-X are fine-tuned for inverse rendering, but it is less clear how pixel-space editors, WeatherWeaver, and rendering methods were tuned or prompted beyond brief descriptions; this affects confidence in the comparative conclusions.

The forward-rendering/control mechanism based on CLIP-space interpolation is useful, but technically heuristic and not deeply analyzed. The paper shows qualitative fine-grained control, yet lacks stronger quantitative evaluation of monotonicity, controllability, or physical consistency across interpolation values.

Several important implementation and reproducibility details appear to be deferred to the supplementary material, including feature distillation details, progressive IMAA training, dataset splits, user-study details, and more ablations. The main paper therefore leaves some uncertainty about whether the results can be independently reproduced.

The method is limited to single images and lacks temporal consistency, which matters directly for autonomous driving video streams. The paper acknowledges this limitation, but it remains a practical weakness for the target application.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: controllable weather editing for autonomous-driving imagery while preserving scene geometry and material identity. The intrinsic-space formulation is well motivated compared with direct pixel-space editing, and the qualitative examples show visibly better preservation of structure and fewer hallucinated changes than several image-editing baselines.

The proposed system is reasonably complete, combining an inverse renderer, a weather-conditioned forward renderer, CLIP-space weather interpolation, feature distillation, and intrinsic map-aware attention. The IMAA ablations show consistent gains on WeatherSynthetic, especially for normal, roughness, metallicity, and irradiance prediction.

The experimental section is broad in scope. It compares against pixel-space editors, weather restoration methods, and inverse/forward rendering methods, and includes downstream detection and segmentation validation on ACDC. The reported improvements on inverse rendering are large on the authors' synthetic benchmark, and user-study preferences strongly favor the proposed method.

The new WeatherSynthetic and WeatherReal datasets, if released as promised, would be useful resources for intrinsic decomposition and weather editing in driving scenes. The dataset construction fills a genuine gap because existing intrinsic-map datasets are mostly indoor or lack weather diversity.
The manuscript is generally clear and well illustrated. The decomposition/re-rendering pipeline, failure cases, and limitations around temporal consistency are understandable.
weaknesses: The strongest quantitative inverse-rendering results are on the authors' own synthetic dataset, whose generation process and distribution are also central to training. This makes the very large gains over prior work difficult to interpret as general capability rather than adaptation to the new synthetic domain. Real-world inverse-rendering evaluation is almost entirely qualitative because ground truth intrinsic maps are unavailable.

WeatherReal relies on pseudo-labels produced by the authors' own inverse renderer, then is used to improve the model. This creates a circular supervision issue: the dataset may encode the model's own biases, and the paper does not provide enough independent validation of pseudo-label accuracy or filtering quality beyond manual checks and examples.

Some comparisons are not fully convincing. Several baselines are not designed for weather/intrinsic driving scenes, while only selected baselines are fine-tuned. The pixel-space comparison table also shows competitors with better DINO structural similarity or comparable PickScore in some settings, so claims of broad superiority should be more carefully qualified.

The downstream ACDC validation is interesting but under-controlled. The paper reports DETR and Segformer gains after re-rendering images, but does not clearly establish that label semantics are preserved in all edits, does not compare quantitatively against restoration/editing baselines on the same downstream protocol, and uses off-the-shelf models whose training weather/domain may already favor sunny-looking outputs.

The forward-rendering and fine-grained control evaluation is still mostly qualitative or preference-based. There is no strong paired-weather benchmark demonstrating that intermediate CLIP interpolation corresponds to calibrated physical weather intensity, and the distillation/interpolation claims are supported mainly by visual examples.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a system of this scale. The paper gives training hardware and some hyperparameters, but the exact dataset generation recipe, prompts, asset composition, filtering criteria, split definitions, and baseline adaptation settings would need to be released carefully for the reported results to be reproducible.

There are presentation and consistency issues, including WeatherSynthetic being described as 38K, 35K, and 35 thousand images in different places, a few unclear equations for the attention bias indexing, and minor wording errors such as 'feature abolition' instead of distillation. These do not undermine the main idea but reduce confidence in the polish of the submission.

The method is single-image only and explicitly lacks temporal consistency. For autonomous-driving weather editing, video coherence is a significant practical requirement, so this limitation materially narrows the immediate usefulness of the approach.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem: controllable weather editing for driving scenes, where preserving geometry and material identity matters for perception systems.

The intrinsic-space formulation is sensible and potentially useful. Separating weather-invariant maps from weather/illumination-dependent irradiance is a clearer control interface than direct pixel-space editing.

The manuscript includes a reasonably broad set of comparisons against pixel-space editors, weather restoration methods, and inverse/forward rendering baselines, plus ablations for IMAA, WeatherSynthetic/WeatherReal, and feature distillation.
The proposed datasets, if released with usable annotations and splits, could be valuable for the community because outdoor weather-diverse intrinsic-map data is scarce.

Qualitative examples suggest that the method can produce visually plausible weather removal/synthesis results and that the inverse renderer may be more robust to adverse weather than indoor-oriented intrinsic decomposition baselines.
weaknesses: The main empirical support is not strong enough for the claims. Quantitative inverse-rendering gains are primarily measured on the authors' own synthetic dataset, whose rendering distribution may closely match the training setup. For real-world data, evaluation is mostly qualitative because no real ground truth intrinsic maps exist.

WeatherReal is methodologically problematic: pseudo-labels are generated by the authors' own inverse renderer and weather variants are produced using Flux-Kontext, then used for finetuning. This creates circular supervision and makes it hard to know whether the model learns physically meaningful intrinsic decomposition or simply distills artifacts from its own pipeline and another editor.

The weather-editing metrics are weak proxies for the stated goals. PickScore, CLIP-S, and DINO-S do not directly measure physical correctness, material preservation, geometry preservation, or weather realism. The reported table is also mixed: Flux-Kontext has much higher DINO-S and Qwen-Image-Edit has higher PickScore, yet the paper argues superiority largely from qualitative judgments.

The downstream ACDC experiment is not fully convincing. Editing validation images to a sunny condition and then evaluating off-the-shelf DETR/SegFormer may improve apparent recognition, but the paper does not establish that labels remain valid after generative edits, that no task-relevant content is hallucinated/removed, or that this is preferable to standard restoration/adaptation baselines under a fair protocol.

Several important implementation and evaluation details remain under-specified despite the supplement: dataset splits, baseline tuning details, prompt construction fairness, exact sampling settings, statistical variation, user-study interface/randomization details beyond a brief description, and whether all baselines use comparable resolution and conditioning.

The IMAA contribution appears incremental and somewhat heuristic. It relies on DINO features, learned map embeddings, manually designed pretraining masks, and a progressive training recipe; the paper shows ablations, but does not deeply justify why the mechanism is technically necessary compared with simpler spatial conditioning or attention-control alternatives.

The claimed physical disentanglement is not adequately validated. Good-looking albedo/normal/roughness images and synthetic PSNR do not prove that weather effects are isolated in irradiance or that materials remain invariant under real adverse weather.

There are consistency and presentation issues that reduce confidence: WeatherSynthetic is described as 38k images in the abstract but 35k in the supplement/table, the dataset release is only promised, and some phrasing/figure references are rough. These are not the core reason for rejection, but they compound reproducibility concerns.

The method is single-image only and explicitly lacks temporal consistency, which is a major limitation for autonomous-driving weather editing. The paper positions downstream driving robustness as a key motivation, but does not provide video-level or sequence-level stability evidence.

Overall, the paper has a promising idea and potentially useful assets, but the evidence does not yet substantiate the strong claims of physically grounded, controllable, and robust weather editing in real driving scenes. The balance therefore favors weak rejection rather than acceptance.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant and useful problem: controllable weather editing for driving scenes, where preserving geometry and material consistency matters for downstream perception. Moving the edit into an intrinsic representation is a sensible design choice and is well motivated against pixel-space weather editing.

The overall system is technically coherent. The separation into inverse rendering, intrinsic maps, and prompt-conditioned forward rendering gives interpretable control, and the intrinsic map-aware attention mechanism is a plausible contribution for improving decomposition of small and distant outdoor structures.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad. The paper compares against pixel-space editors, weather restoration methods, and rendering-based methods; reports perceptual/text/structure metrics, inverse-rendering metrics, downstream ACDC detection/segmentation results, qualitative comparisons, user preference, and ablations for IMAA, WeatherReal, and distillation.

The results are generally strong. On WeatherSynthetic, the inverse renderer substantially outperforms adapted baselines across albedo, normal, roughness, metallicity, and irradiance metrics, and the downstream ACDC experiment shows meaningful gains for DETR and Segformer after weather normalization.

The dataset contribution is potentially valuable. WeatherSynthetic and WeatherReal target a clear gap: outdoor autonomous-driving scenes with diverse weather and intrinsic-map supervision, rather than indoor/object-centric intrinsic datasets.

The manuscript is mostly clear and well organized. The figures communicate the motivation and the qualitative advantages effectively, and the limitations section candidly notes lack of temporal consistency.
weaknesses: The strongest quantitative intrinsic-rendering evidence is on the authors' own synthetic dataset, which is also the domain used to train the method. This makes the very large PSNR/SSIM gains less conclusive about real-world decomposition quality, especially since real-world intrinsic maps are pseudo-labels rather than ground truth.

WeatherReal is generated using the authors' inverse renderer and then used for finetuning, which creates a partially circular supervision pipeline. The paper states that quality is manually checked, but does not provide enough detail about filtering criteria, error rates, or how pseudo-label bias affects the forward renderer.

The comparison to recent large image editors is useful but not fully decisive. PickScore, CLIP-S, and DINO-S are imperfect proxies for physically correct weather editing, and some claims about hallucination or geometry preservation rely heavily on selected qualitative examples. More controlled human evaluation details and failure statistics would strengthen the case.

The downstream ACDC evaluation is promising but somewhat under-specified. Editing validation images into sunny conditions while using the original annotations can be informative, but the paper does not fully analyze whether the editing changes label validity, whether improvements come from weather removal versus distribution shift toward the pretrained detectors, or how this compares to standard restoration/domain-adaptation pipelines.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details such as exact train/test splits, training schedules, batch sizes, compute, all prompt templates, baseline tuning protocols, and the manual curation process are not sufficiently specified in the main text. The dataset is promised for release, but the review must evaluate the current manuscript.

There are several presentation and consistency issues: WeatherSynthetic is described as 38k images in the abstract/main contribution but 35k in the supplement; some appendix text has typos or awkward phrases; and parts of the method, especially CLIP-space interpolation and feature distillation, are described at a high level without enough implementation detail to reproduce exactly.

The novelty is solid but not transformative. The work combines known components, including Stable Diffusion finetuning, intrinsic decomposition, DINO-based attention guidance, CLIP interpolation, and pseudo-labeled real data. The main contribution is the effective adaptation and integration for weather editing rather than a fundamentally new generative modeling principle.
